summary: Internet mail was limited to 7-bit ASCII, and MIME added 8-bit body support and encoded-words for some header values. This RFC permits Unicode directly in email headers, including addresses, for full internationalization.

eli5.summary: Mail labels used to allow only simple letters. This lets labels be written in any language, using all kinds of characters.

subtitle: Lets email headers and addresses use UTF-8 directly, with no encoded-word tricks.

tldr.problem: Email headers were limited to 7-bit ASCII. MIME encoded-words allowed other characters only in some header places, were complex, and invited processing errors.
tldr.mechanism: The header grammar of RFC 5322 is extended so UTF-8 may appear in most header field values and in addresses, and a new media type, message/global, labels such messages.
tldr.outcome: Such messages need the SMTPUTF8 extension to travel over SMTP. The RFC obsoletes RFC 5335 and updates a MIME rule about encoding message subtypes.

today: RFC 6532 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. It obsoletes RFC 5335 and updates RFC 2045, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It is meant to be used with RFC 6531.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Internet mail separates a message from its transport and splits a message into header and body. Header field values hold many strings meant for people to read, but their characters were originally limited to 7-bit ASCII. MIME allowed other character sets in body parts and, through encoded-words, in a limited number of header places.

The RFC argues that globalization needs Unicode in both addresses and most header values, that encoded-words add inefficiency and chances for processing errors, and that UTF-8 is now natively available on most systems. So it specifies direct use of UTF-8 in header field values, including mail addresses.

The design assumes native, end-to-end UTF-8 support in an 8-bit-clean environment. Carrying such mail over legacy 7-bit infrastructure is not covered here. The document replaces RFC 5335, and RFC 6530 describes the change in approach.
sections.eli5: Letters used to be written with only a small set of plain symbols. Now you may write your name exactly as it is spelled in your own language.

sections.title: Syntax Extensions to RFC 5322
sections.content:
The header grammar is widened by adding UTF8-non-ascii to several RFC 5322 rules: VCHAR, ctext, atext, qtext, text and dtext. The rule for text also upgrades the body to UTF-8.

In practice UTF-8 is now allowed in unstructured text such as Subject: and Content-description:, in anything built from atoms (including local parts of addresses, Message-IDs and the for clauses of Received:), in quoted strings, and in domains.

Header field names do not change: they must still be ASCII only. Messages in this format need the SMTPUTF8 extension of RFC 6531 to travel by SMTP.
sections.eli5: The words inside the label may use any letters. The names of the label boxes, like To and From, stay in plain letters.

sections.title: UTF-8 and Normalization
sections.content:
UTF-8 characters are defined in terms of octets using the rules of RFC 3629. The RFC discusses Unicode normalization and says that normalization form NFC SHOULD be used. The NFKC form SHOULD NOT be used, because it may lose information needed to spell some names correctly. Since many mailbox local parts reflect personal names, the stated goal of letting people spell their names correctly applies to mailboxes too.

Message-ID generators MAY prefer ASCII output. That helps with In-reply-to: and References: in mailing-list threads where some senders use internationalized addresses and others do not.
sections.eli5: The same letter can sometimes be written in more than one way on a computer. The rules say to use the standard way that keeps names spelled correctly.

sections.title: Line Length and MIME Changes
sections.content:
RFC 5322 limits lines to 998 characters and recommends 78. This RFC changes the first limit to 998 octets, because in UTF-8 octets and characters are no longer the same thing. The 78 limit stays in characters, since it concerns display width, not line length.

It also updates Section 6.4 of RFC 2045. That rule prohibited any content-transfer-encoding on subtypes of message/. The prohibition is relaxed: newly defined MIME types may permit it, and message/global does. Normally message/global travels over 8-bit-clean channels with identity encoding. But if a message is downgraded from 8-bit to 7-bit as in RFC 6152, an encoding may need to be applied, and several levels may nest if the message crosses between environments more than once. The RFC expects this to be rarely seen.
sections.eli5: Fancy letters can take more space than plain ones, so the length limit is now counted in bytes rather than letters.

sections.title: Encoded-Words and the message/global Type
sections.content:
Encoded-words SHOULD NOT be used when generating headers for messages that use this extension. Agents MAY convert encoded-words to direct UTF-8 when incorporating material from another message, but anyone who decodes them MUST NOT generate syntactically invalid fields.

A message is a message/global message if it has 8-bit UTF-8 header values, either at the top level or in the header fields of body parts. Its content is otherwise identical to message/rfc822. It MUST only be transmitted as authorized by RFC 6531 or within a non-SMTP environment that supports such messages. Sent to a 7-bit-only system, it MUST have a content-transfer-encoding applied. A MIME system that does not recognize the type treats it as application/octet-stream.

When embedding such content in another message, one may keep the message/global type or down-convert to message/rfc822. Both interoperate with the installed base but differ in properties: unaware systems see message/global as an unknown attachment, while systems that understand it give better results than a down-converted copy.
sections.eli5: The old trick for writing fancy letters in a label is now discouraged. A special sticker, message/global, tells everyone a letter has the new kind of label.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
UTF-8 often needs several octets per character, so header values and addresses can get longer. The 998-octet line limit still applies. Mail Delivery Agent processes that handle addresses must take care not to overflow buffers, truncate addresses or exceed storage, and must compare entire lengths.

There are many ways to use UTF-8 to represent something equivalent to a displayed character, which RFC 3629 describes as a problem. The normalization process of the earlier section is recommended to minimize these issues. The effect on signature systems such as DKIM, S/MIME and OpenPGP is discussed in RFC 6530. A certificate for a user with both ASCII and non-ASCII addresses might list both, which PKIX and OpenPGP already support, though user-interface issues may arise.

IANA updated the registration of the message/global media type. The registration suggests the extension .u8msg and, for Macintosh, the uniform type identifier public.utf8-email-message.
sections.eli5: Longer names can overflow small boxes, and look-alike letters can fool people. So programs must check carefully and use the standard spelling form.
